migrationNotes: Spine: we start with an odometer's average speed, turn it into the slope of a line across a curve, then shrink the stretch and watch that slope settle on one number, which is the rate at a single instant.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): cal-from-secant-to-tangent-3 and -11 (the limit definition as a multiple choice, and one more average rate; both are covered by the worked and faded examples).

lesson.title: From average rate to instant rate

lead.text: A rate compares two changes. A tank holds 20 litres at the 2 minute mark and 50 litres at the 5 minute mark. The contents rose by 30 litres while the time rose by 3 minutes, so on average the tank filled at 30 ÷ 3 = 10 litres per minute.

Every average rate has this shape: the change in the output divided by the change in the input. It describes the whole stretch. The tank may have filled quickly at first and slowly later, and the average hides that.
Here f(a) and f(b) are the outputs at the start and end of the stretch, and b − a is its length. We write f for any function, and a and b for two chosen inputs.

lead.text: Back to the odometer from the start of the lesson.

reveal.text: You divided the change in distance by the change in time. That is an average rate, and it says nothing about any single moment.

lead.text: The same idea works on a graph. Take the curve y = x² and pick two points on it, at x = 0 and x = 2. The heights are 0 and 4, so the average rate between them is (4 − 0) ÷ (2 − 0) = 2. That number is also the slope of the straight line through the two points, because the rise is 4 and the run is 2.
A line drawn through two points of a curve is called a secant. Its slope is the average rate over the stretch between the points, and a steep secant means the curve climbs quickly over that stretch.

afterFigure.text: Use the buttons to compare a wide stretch with a narrower one, and drag the slider to shrink the stretch. The secant turns as its second point slides towards the first, and the slope reported under the picture changes with it. Keep an eye on that turning, because the rest of the lesson builds on it.

lead.text: Work out an average rate on the same curve, this time between x = 1 and x = 3.

reveal.text: You divided the change in height by the change in input. That is the slope of the secant, and it belongs to the whole stretch.

lead.text: To get the rate at one point, say x = 1 on y = x², we need a second point to draw the secant through, and then we move it closer. Call the second point 1 + h, where h is the width of the stretch. The height at x = 1 is 1.

Try some widths. With h = 1 the slope is (4 − 1) ÷ 1 = 3. Halve the width to h = 0.5 and it becomes (2.25 − 1) ÷ 0.5 = 2.5. At h = 0.1 it is (1.21 − 1) ÷ 0.1 = 2.1. The slopes fall towards 2 as the stretch shrinks.

afterFigure.text: We cannot set h = 0 to get the slope exactly, because that would be 0 ÷ 0, the same trouble as the gap in the first lesson. The way out is the same too. The slope at the point is the limit of the secant slopes as h approaches 0, and a limit never needs h to be 0.

steps.headline: Find the slope of the secant for f(x) = x² from x = 1 to x = 1 + h, as h approaches 0.

workedSteps.text: Divide by h. Allowed, because h is never zero.

steps.headline: Find the slope of the secant for f(x) = x² from x = 2 to x = 2 + h, as h approaches 0.

lead.text: The worked lines show the pattern. The h that gets in the way vanishes as h shrinks, and what remains is the limit of the secant slopes. At x = 1 it was 2, and at x = 2 it was 4.

That limit is the derivative of the function at the point, written f′(a) for the point x = a. It is the instantaneous rate of change, the rate at that single instant. On the graph it is the slope of the tangent, the line that just touches the curve at the point. As the second point slides in, the secant swings round into the tangent.

A derivative carries a sign. A positive derivative means the function is rising at that point, and a negative one means it is falling. It is also a different thing from the height. Saying f(4) = 7 and f′(4) = −2 describes a curve at height 7 that is falling by 2 units for each unit moved to the right.

afterFigure.text: Drag the slider to slide the tangent along the curve y = x². On the left of the bottom the tangent tilts down and its slope is negative, and on the right it tilts up. For this curve the slope reported is always twice the x value.

lead.text: Same method, a different point: x = 5. The secant slope has already been simplified for you.

reveal.text: The same move again: let the h term vanish and keep what is left. That limit is the derivative at 5.

lead.text: From x = 3 to x = 4 the secant slope of x² is 7. That averages the whole stretch, so the rate right at 3 can differ.

reveal.text: The rate at x = 3 is 6, below the average of 7 over the next unit, because the curve is still steepening.

lesson.orientation: Turn average rates over an interval into a derivative at a point.

blocks.text: A car's odometer reads 40 km at 1:00 and 100 km at 2:30. From those two readings you can say how far the car went and how long it took, and so how fast it went on average. What the readings cannot tell you is how fast the car was going at 2:00 exactly.

That second question is harder than it looks. Speed is distance divided by time, but at a single instant no time passes and no distance is covered. The speed at an instant looks like 0 ÷ 0. The last two lessons showed what to do with 0 ÷ 0: stop standing on the point and look at what happens close to it.

This lesson starts with an average over a stretch and then shrinks the stretch. The average settles on a single number, which is the rate at one instant. The same method gives the steepness of a curve at one point.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn secant slopes into a derivative, and read it as the rate at one point.
intro.whyItMatters: Speed, growth and slope at an instant are all derivatives.

recap.keyIdea: The derivative at a point is the limit of the secant slopes as the stretch shrinks: the rate at that instant.

blocks.text: Back at the odometer, you turned two readings into an average speed and then replaced the two readings with a shrinking stretch. You found an average rate of 4 for x² between 1 and 3, then watched the slope settle on 2 at x = 1 and on 4 at x = 2.

recap.nextHook: Working out each slope as a limit takes a page of algebra. In the next lesson we'll tabulate the slopes of y = x² and look for a pattern that does the work for us.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², find the average rate from x = 1 to x = 3.
hints: Divide the output change by the input change.
Compute both endpoint heights by squaring.
Subtract those heights and divide by the difference between the inputs.
questions.onCorrect: 4. Change in height over change in input: the slope of the secant joining the two points.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 is the change in height. Divide by the change in input as well.

questions.prompt: At x = 2, the secant slope for f(x) = x² is 4 + h. What does it approach as h approaches 0?
hints: Let the nonzero interval become arbitrarily small.
The formula separates a constant part and a shrinking part.
Remove the term that tends to zero and retain the constant part.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The extra h tends to zero, leaving slope 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The extra h shrinks to zero and the constant part is what the slopes head for.

misconceptions.feedback: The h term tends to 0, but the constant part stays.

questions.prompt: How is a derivative at a point obtained from secant slopes?
hints: A height and a rate of change describe different things.

acceptedIdeas: Take their limit as the interval shrinks
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The derivative is the limiting slope, provided the limit exists.

choices.label: Take their limit as the interval shrinks
Substitute zero into the unsimplified denominator
Use the height of the graph

questions.onCorrect: Take the limit of the secant slopes. The limit avoids dividing by zero.

misconceptions.feedback: Putting h = 0 into the unsimplified quotient divides by zero. A limit gets round that.
A height and a rate are different things. The derivative is a slope.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², f′(x) = 2x. Find the instantaneous rate at x = 3.
hints: Use the rate function, not the original height function.
The derivative formula already describes the instantaneous rate.
Evaluate that formula at the requested input.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Evaluate the rate formula at the point: 2 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 3 is the input. Put it into the rate formula 2x.
9 is the height f(3). The question asks for the rate.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², find the average rate from x = 2 to x = 5.
hints: Use the two endpoint values.
Square each endpoint to find its height.
Divide the difference of heights by the difference of inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The output change is 25 − 4 = 21 over input change 3, so the rate is 7.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Change in height, 25 − 4, over change in input, 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 21 is the change in height. Divide by the change in input as well.

questions.prompt: A function has f(2) = 9 and f′(2) = −3. Which statement describes its instantaneous rate?
hints: Distinguish the function value from its derivative.

acceptedIdeas: It is falling at 3 output units per input unit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The derivative −3 gives the signed local rate; 9 is the height.

choices.label: It is falling at 3 output units per input unit
It is rising at nine units per input unit

questions.onCorrect: f′(2) = −3 is a rate with a sign: negative means falling, 3 units per input unit.

misconceptions.feedback: −3 is the derivative, not the height. The height is f(2).
9 is the height, not the rate. The sign of the derivative also matters.

questions.prompt: A car's odometer reads 40 km at 1:00 and 100 km at 2:30. What was its average speed in km per hour?
hints: How far did the car travel between the two readings?
How long did that take, from 1:00 to 2:30?
Divide the distance by the time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The car covered 100 − 40 = 60 km in 1.5 hours, and 60 ÷ 1.5 = 40.

questions.onCorrect: 40. Change in distance over change in time is an average rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance. Divide it by the time taken as well.
The trip took 1.5 hours, from 1:00 to 2:30, not 3.

questions.prompt: Why can't we just put h = 0 into (1 + h)² − 1 over h?
hints: What would the bottom of the fraction be?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At h = 0 the bottom is 0, and division by zero is undefined.

choices.label: The top would not be zero

questions.onCorrect: Putting in h = 0 divides by zero. Simplify first, then take the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: h is a small step that gets smaller, not a fixed number.
Try it: with h = 0 the top is 1² − 1, which is 0 as well. Look at the bottom.

questions.prompt: At x = 5, the secant slope for f(x) = x² is 10 + h. What does it approach as h approaches 0?
hints: Which part of the slope gets smaller as h shrinks?
One part tends to zero as h does.
What is left when that part is gone?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The h term shrinks to zero, leaving 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. The shrinking h term vanishes and the constant part is the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is where x sits, not the slope. Look at what the slope expression tends to.
The h part tends to zero, but the constant part stays.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², f′(x) = 2x. At which x is the instantaneous rate equal to 10?
hints: The rate at x is f′(x) = 2x. What do you want it to equal?
Solve 2x = 10.
Divide both sides by 2.
questions.onCorrect: 5. The derivative is a rate function: set it equal to 10 and solve for x.

misconceptions.feedback: 20 is 2 × 10. You need the x that makes 2x equal 10.
That is the height of the curve at the key point. The question is about the rate.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², what is the average rate from x = 1 to x = 2?
hints: Find the height at each end first.
The heights are 1 and 4. What is the change?
Divide that change by the change in input.
questions.onCorrect: 3. Change in height, 4 − 1, over change in input, 1.

misconceptions.feedback: 4 is the height at the right end. Subtract the left height and divide by the change in input.

citations.claim: An average rate is the change in output divided by the change in input over a stretch.

The secant slope of x² from 2 to 2 + h simplifies to 4 + h, whose limit is 4.
The derivative at a point is the limit of the secant slopes as the interval shrinks: the instantaneous rate, the slope of the tangent, positive when rising and negative when falling.
